Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing says true love like releasing a caged butterfly, don't you think? Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are to be paid $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are reported to be the piece-de-resistance of England's most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year. Wayne Rooney, the best English footballer of his generation, and Coleen McLoughlin, his High School sweetheart, were to marry in an estimated $10 million ceremony in Italy Thursday. As they kiss, guests are apparently meant to open boxes and release the butterflies. The moment has been pilloried widely in the British media, tacky and over the top they all think, but is it just sour grapes? It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road for the couple to the altar. One littered with fierce criticism from the British press, which has enjoyed nothing more than lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin for being 'common.' The Daily Mail once even asked: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" due to his looks and his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often referred to in a disparaging way. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page upon page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and her lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. There has also been fierce criticism over the fact she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. It's all down to Rooney apparently, and nothing to do with her appearing to be quite a decent person, who did well at school and has cleverly managed to parlay some of her fame into various media and advertising projects. Anyone who has seen her television show -- Coleen's Real Women -- can see she is a decent, bubbly person, who is very good at putting people at ease. Much to the media's fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to OK magazine for a record $5 million. However they're not pocketing all the cash themselves, with an undisclosed sum from the fee to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire -- where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister Rosie is cared for. The queen's grandson, Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly, recently received $1m from Hello magazine to cover their wedding but they didn't receive an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous, but lower class, Rooney and McLoughlin. Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have also asked guests to donate money to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool. The wedding might be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests (they are covering the guests' costs), expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress, but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for critics. It's just not on that someone who wasn't born into privilege and didn't go to a posh school can enjoy their wealth. That would be ugly. If anything, the couple's relationship and success is a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, but she spent two years fending off Rooney's entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question again and got a yes. Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairytale complete with butterflies? The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

outputs.L1:
LONDON, England (CNN) — Nothing says true love quite like the release of a caged butterfly, does it?

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are reportedly to be paid $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are said to be the pièce de résistance of England’s most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year.

Rooney, widely regarded as the best English footballer of his generation, and McLoughlin, his high school sweetheart, were due to marry Thursday in Italy in a ceremony estimated to cost $10 million. As the couple kiss, guests are apparently expected to open boxes and release the butterflies.

The gesture has been widely pilloried in the British media as tacky and over the top. But is the criticism simply a case of sour grapes?

It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road to the altar for the couple — one marked by fierce criticism from the British press, which has often seemed to take particular pleasure in lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin as “common.” The Daily Mail once even asked: “Is this Britain’s ghastliest couple?”

Rooney has been dubbed “Shrek” and “Mr Potato Head” because of his looks, while his background — as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate — is often invoked in a disparaging way.

McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page after page of unkind stories about her weight, her shopping sprees, and her perceived lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. She has also faced sharp criticism for having become a millionaire in her own right. Apparently, that achievement is entirely down to Rooney and has nothing to do with her seeming to be a thoroughly decent person who did well at school and has astutely turned some of her fame into various media and advertising projects.

Anyone who has watched her television show, *Coleen’s Real Women*, can see that she is a warm, bubbly person with a real gift for putting people at ease.

Much to the media’s fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to *OK!* magazine for a record $5 million. However, they are not keeping all of the money themselves: an undisclosed sum from the fee will be donated to Claire House children’s hospice in Cheshire, where McLoughlin’s disabled foster sister, Rosie, is cared for.

The queen’s grandson, Peter Phillips, and his bride, Autumn Kelly, recently received $1 million from *Hello!* magazine to cover their wedding, yet they did not receive even an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous — but lower-class — Rooney and McLoughlin.

Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have asked guests to donate money to Alder Hey children’s hospital in Liverpool.

The wedding may be extravagant, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests — whose costs the couple are covering — expensive wine, and a $200,000 wedding dress. But at least Rooney and McLoughlin have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for their critics. It seems unacceptable to some that someone who was not born into privilege and did not attend an elite school should be able to enjoy wealth. That would be ugly.

If anything, the couple’s relationship and success represent a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, though she spent two years fending off Rooney’s requests for a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, asked again, and this time received a yes.

Surely they deserve to be congratulated for creating their own modern fairy tale — complete with butterflies.

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

That planned moment has been mocked across much of the British press, where many have described it as tasteless and excessive. But could some of the criticism simply be resentment?

For Rooney and McLoughlin, the path to marriage has been lengthy and sometimes difficult. Along the way, they have faced harsh scrutiny from British newspapers, which have often taken pleasure in ridiculing them as “common.” The Daily Mail once went so far as to ask: “Is this Britain’s ghastliest couple?”

Rooney has been called “Shrek” and “Mr Potato Head” because of his appearance, while his upbringing — as the son of a school dinner lady who was raised on a council estate — is frequently mentioned in sneering terms.

McLoughlin, for her part, has endured endless hostile coverage about her weight, her shopping habits and her supposedly distant relationship with Victoria Beckham. She has also been sharply criticized for becoming a millionaire in her own right.

Apparently, critics believe that achievement is entirely because of Rooney, rather than acknowledging that McLoughlin seems to be a perfectly decent person who performed well at school and has shrewdly turned some of her public profile into media and advertising opportunities.

Anyone who has watched her television program, “Coleen’s Real Women,” can see that she comes across as warm, lively and skilled at helping others feel comfortable.

To the irritation of much of the media, the couple sold the rights to cover their wedding to OK! magazine for a record $5 million. But they are not keeping the entire sum. An undisclosed portion of the fee is being donated to Claire House children’s hospice in Cheshire, where McLoughlin’s disabled foster sister, Rosie, is cared for.

Recently, Peter Phillips, the Queen’s grandson, and his wife Autumn Kelly received $1 million from Hello! magazine for coverage of their wedding. Yet they attracted nowhere near the level of condemnation now aimed at Rooney and McLoughlin, who are giving more generously but come from a less privileged background.

In addition, instead of wedding gifts, Rooney and McLoughlin have asked their guests to contribute money to Alder Hey children’s hospital in Liverpool.

The celebration may well be extravagant, featuring a private yacht, luxury jet travel for guests — with the couple paying their guests’ expenses — costly wine and a $200,000 wedding dress. Still, they have earned what they have through their own efforts.

What seems to bother their critics most is that they have succeeded despite their working-class roots. The idea that people who were not born into privilege and did not attend elite schools might enjoy their fortune appears, to some, to be unacceptable. That attitude is the truly unpleasant one.

If anything, Rooney and McLoughlin’s relationship and achievements amount to a victory over difficult circumstances. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, although she spent two years turning down Rooney’s attempts to persuade her to go on a date.

He eventually got his opportunity when he saw her having trouble repairing a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, asked her out again, and this time she agreed.

Surely, then, they deserve congratulations for building their own modern fairy tale — butterflies included.

The views expressed in this commentary belong solely to the writer.

Rooney, one of the most famous footballers in Britain, and McLoughlin, already a celebrity in her own right after years in the public eye, were never likely to marry quietly in a village church followed by a modest reception. Their Italian celebration was reported as lavish, expensive, and carefully managed for the cameras. Yet the reaction to it revealed as much about the British media as it did about the couple themselves.

Much of the press coverage focused on the more extravagant details of the event. Newspapers and commentators seized on reports of a butterfly release, designer clothes, luxury hotels, private transport, and a lucrative magazine deal for the wedding photographs. The reported $5 million arrangement for exclusive photo rights became a particular target. To many critics, it was presented as proof that the couple were vulgar, excessive, or somehow lacking in taste. The wedding was treated not simply as a private celebration, but as a public offence.

But the level of hostility was striking. Celebrity weddings are often expensive, carefully staged, and sold to magazines. Wealthy actors, singers, models, and aristocrats have done the same without attracting quite the same sneering tone. In Rooney and McLoughlin’s case, however, the coverage often seemed less like genuine criticism of extravagance and more like an excuse to mock them. Every detail was held up as evidence that they had too much money and not enough refinement.

That attitude points to a deeper issue: class snobbery. Rooney and McLoughlin came from working-class backgrounds, and their success did not fit comfortably with the expectations of certain commentators. Rooney’s football talent brought him enormous wealth at a young age, while McLoughlin became famous through her relationship with him and through her own celebrity profile. For sections of the press, this combination made them easy targets. They were rich, visible, and popular, but they were not seen as possessing the “right” kind of polish.

The criticism of the wedding therefore seemed to carry an implied message: people like them should not spend money in such a public way. Their wealth was treated differently from inherited wealth or more culturally approved forms of celebrity success. When the very rich stage grand weddings in castles or country estates, the coverage is often admiring or romantic. When Rooney and McLoughlin did something similar, it was described as tacky, tasteless, and absurd.

The butterfly release became a symbol of this reaction. It was mocked as though it represented everything supposedly ridiculous about the wedding. Yet in reality, it was just one decorative gesture at a celebrity event. The outrage surrounding it was disproportionate. It was not the butterflies themselves that bothered people; it was what they were made to represent. They became a shorthand for the idea that the couple had more money than sophistication.

Similarly, the photo-rights deal was portrayed as greedy or cynical, even though such arrangements are common in celebrity culture. Selling exclusive photographs can also be a way of controlling access and limiting the intrusion of paparazzi. For a couple already subjected to intense scrutiny, it was hardly surprising that they would prefer one controlled media deal to a chaotic free-for-all. Yet this practical explanation was largely ignored in favour of moral condemnation.

The backlash also showed the uneasy relationship Britain has with fame, money, and social mobility. Rooney’s footballing ability made him a national hero when he scored goals, but his personal life was often treated as fair game for ridicule. McLoughlin, meanwhile, was frequently dismissed or patronised, despite building a recognisable public identity of her own. Their popularity with many ordinary fans did not protect them from a media culture eager to cut them down.

What made the criticism especially unfair was that the couple had not done anything particularly shocking. They had spent their own money, celebrated their marriage, and made a commercial agreement in a media environment that constantly demands access to celebrities’ private lives. The same newspapers that complained about the sale of the wedding photographs were also eager to report every detail of the event. The outrage was therefore difficult to take at face value.

In the end, the reaction to Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding was less about butterflies, dresses, hotels, or magazine rights than about resentment. It exposed a familiar pattern in British tabloid culture: build people up, profit from their fame, and then mock them for enjoying the rewards of that fame. Rooney and McLoughlin were presented as symbols of excess, but the harshness of the response revealed more about the prejudices of their critics than about the couple themselves.

Their wedding may have been lavish, but lavish celebrity weddings are not unusual. What was unusual was the intensity of the sneering directed at them. Beneath the jokes and moralising lay an old-fashioned discomfort with working-class people becoming rich, confident, and visible. The criticism pretended to be about taste, but it often sounded much more like class contempt.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style opinion commentary defending Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s lavish Italian wedding, including the butterfly release, media criticism, class prejudice, charity donations, and their long relationship.
counterfactuals.output:
**Opinion: Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding was lavish. So what?**

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s Italian wedding was never going to be a quiet parish-hall affair. He was one of the most famous footballers in Britain; she had grown up under the harsh glare that comes with dating — and later marrying — a national sporting obsession. Their celebration in Italy, complete with designer touches, a picturesque setting and the much-discussed butterfly release, was always destined to become tabloid fuel.

But the reaction to it said at least as much about Britain’s attitudes to class, fame and money as it did about the couple themselves.

Yes, the wedding was extravagant. Reports at the time dwelled on the cost, the guest list, the location and the spectacle. The butterfly release became an easy symbol for critics: too much, too showy, too “new money.” It was framed as proof of excess, as though a young couple’s wedding choices were a matter of national moral decline.

But this criticism often carried a familiar sting. When aristocrats, heirs or society figures stage lavish weddings, the pageantry is frequently described as tradition, romance or heritage. When a working-class footballer from Liverpool and his childhood sweetheart do it, the tone can shift: vulgar, tasteless, undeserved. The same spending that looks elegant in one context is mocked as gaudy in another.

That double standard matters.

Rooney did not inherit his status. He earned it in one of the most competitive and physically punishing professions in the world, under scrutiny from his teenage years. Coleen, too, became famous young, and endured years of public judgment about her clothes, her spending, her body, her relationship and her choices. If two people who have lived that public life decide to celebrate their marriage in a beautiful Italian setting, why should that provoke outrage?

The answer, in part, is that Britain has always had a complicated relationship with working-class success. It loves the fairytale ascent — until the successful person starts spending like someone who has actually made it. Then admiration curdles into resentment. The message becomes: succeed, but don’t enjoy it too visibly.

The criticism also ignored another important point: the couple’s wedding reportedly included charitable donations and gestures beyond the spectacle. That detail never seemed to travel as far as the jokes about butterflies or the headlines about luxury. Charity does not mean every expensive choice becomes immune from criticism, but it does complicate the caricature of a selfish, thoughtless display.

And then there is the simplest fact of all: this was not a celebrity fling manufactured for publicity. Rooney and McLoughlin had known each other since childhood. Their relationship long predated the mansions, endorsements, magazine deals and international attention. Whatever anyone thinks of the wedding aesthetics, theirs was a long relationship rooted in a shared background and history. That should have counted for something.

Instead, much of the public conversation reduced them to symbols — of footballer excess, “WAG” culture, tabloid celebrity and aspirational spending. Coleen in particular was treated with a sneer often reserved for young women who become famous adjacent to male achievement, as though her choices were uniquely open to national ridicule.

People are entitled to dislike lavish weddings. They are entitled to find butterfly releases theatrical, or to question the culture of celebrity exclusives and high-cost ceremonies. But there is a difference between critiquing excess and policing who is allowed to display success.

Rooney and McLoughlin’s wedding was expensive, sentimental, dramatic and perhaps, to some tastes, over the top. But weddings often are. They are emotional performances of love, family, identity and aspiration. For a couple who had grown up together and come into extraordinary wealth and fame at a young age, a grand celebration was hardly shocking.

The discomfort many expressed was not really about butterflies. It was about boundaries — who gets to be glamorous, who gets to be romantic on a large scale, who gets to spend without being called vulgar.

Wayne and Coleen’s wedding may not have been everyone’s idea of tasteful. It didn’t need to be. It was theirs.

counterfactuals.output:
LONDON, England (CNN) — The reported $5 million sale of Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding photo rights to *OK!* magazine has prompted the familiar chorus of disapproval: too flashy, too commercial, too much money for a private day.

But much of the criticism says less about Rooney and McLoughlin than it does about Britain’s enduring discomfort with young, working-class people becoming very rich, very visible and unapologetically in control of their own celebrity.

Rooney, one of England’s most recognizable footballers, and McLoughlin, already a tabloid fixture in her own right, were never going to have an ordinary wedding. Their lives have been photographed, discussed and picked apart since they were teenagers. In that context, selling the rights to carefully managed wedding pictures is not some shocking surrender of intimacy. It is a rational response to a media culture that would have pursued the images anyway.

The couple faced a choice: allow paparazzi and newspapers to profit from stolen glimpses, or make a deal on their own terms. They chose the latter. That is not vulgarity. It is business.

The sneering tone surrounding the deal is revealing. When aristocrats, actors or society figures monetize access to their lives, it is often packaged as glamour, branding or clever image management. When a footballer from Croxteth and his childhood sweetheart do the same, it is treated as evidence of bad taste.

That double standard is hard to miss.

Of course, nobody needs to feel sentimental about a multimillion-dollar magazine contract. Rooney and McLoughlin are wealthy public figures, and celebrity weddings are part of a commercial machine that can be gaudy and excessive. But criticism of the system is different from moralizing about the couple personally.

The public appetite for celebrity spectacle created this market. Magazines pay huge sums because readers buy the issues, advertisers follow the readers and the images become valuable commodities. To condemn Rooney and McLoughlin for accepting the money while consuming the coverage is a convenient form of hypocrisy.

There is also a class element in the way “taste” is policed. The objection is rarely just that the wedding photographs were sold. It is that they were sold by people perceived as insufficiently refined to be so wealthy, so famous and so confident about cashing in. In Britain especially, money is often more acceptable when it is inherited quietly than earned loudly.

Rooney’s career has been built on rare talent under intense pressure. McLoughlin’s celebrity has been shaped by the same tabloid ecosystem that now criticizes her for using it. Their wedding deal may be extravagant, but it is hardly irrational. If anything, it shows a clear understanding of the marketplace around them.

The discomfort, then, is not really about one magazine contract. It is about who is allowed to profit from fame without being mocked for it.

Rooney and McLoughlin did not invent celebrity culture, the paparazzi economy or the public fascination with footballers’ private lives. They simply recognized their value within it. For that, they have been accused of tackiness.

A fairer verdict might be this: they played the game as it exists — and won.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an editorial on England’s celebrity wedding of the year: Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s $10 million ceremony in Italy, the British press mocking them as tacky and “common,” and why the couple deserve sympathy and congratulations.
counterfactuals.output:
**In Defence of Wayne and Coleen’s Big, Brash Wedding**

England has found its celebrity wedding of the year, and—predictably—it has also found something to sneer at.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s lavish Italian ceremony, reportedly costing around $10 million, has been treated in parts of the British press less as a marriage than as a national embarrassment. The verdict from the sneering classes has been swift: too flashy, too expensive, too “tacky,” too “common.” The implication is unmistakable. This was not merely criticism of a celebrity spectacle; it was class disdain dressed up as taste.

Of course, it is easy to mock excess. A multimillion-dollar wedding in Italy, private jets, designer dresses, celebrity guests and glossy magazine deals are hardly symbols of restraint. In an age when many families are struggling, such extravagance can feel jarring. Public figures who sell access to their private lives cannot be surprised when the public has opinions about the result.

But there is something unpleasant about the tone of the ridicule directed at Rooney and McLoughlin. Much of it has not really been about money at all. Britain is perfectly capable of admiring wealth when it comes wrapped in aristocratic understatement, old-family privilege or the right accent. What seems to offend some commentators is not that the couple spent a fortune, but that they spent it in a way that did not ask permission from people who believe they are the guardians of good taste.

Rooney and McLoughlin are, in many ways, a very modern British success story. They are young, famous, rich and from working-class Liverpool backgrounds. Their lives have been scrutinised since their teens. Coleen, in particular, has grown up in the public eye while being patronised as a footballer’s girlfriend, a shopper, a tabloid figure—rarely granted the dignity of being treated as a young woman navigating extraordinary attention. Rooney, for all his fame and sporting brilliance, has often been caricatured rather than understood.

So when they marry, they do what many young couples would do if given a fortune and a fantasy: they make the day enormous. They take their families abroad. They celebrate loudly. They turn private happiness into public theatre because public theatre is the world they inhabit. It may not be subtle, but why must it be? Not every wedding has to look like a tasteful country-house reception approved by newspaper columnists.

The charge of being “common” is particularly revealing. It is one of those words that says more about the person using it than about its target. It pretends to be a judgment about manners, but it usually means: know your place. Do not spend too much. Do not sparkle too brightly. Do not bring your relatives, your accent, your preferences and your joy into spaces where others believe refinement belongs only to them.

There is also a basic human fact being lost amid the mockery: two young people who have known each other since childhood have got married. Behind the magazine spreads and designer labels is a relationship that predates the fame, the money and the circus. That alone is rare in the world they now occupy. Celebrity can corrode trust, distort ordinary life and turn every mistake into a headline. If Rooney and McLoughlin have chosen to make a commitment to each other under such pressure, the decent response is not contempt but goodwill.

They deserve congratulations not because the wedding was modest, but because marriage is not a performance review. They deserve sympathy because their happiness has been filtered through a press culture that often profits from excess and then condemns it. Newspapers help create the celebrity economy, bid for the pictures, inflate the spectacle, and then tut when the spectacle looks gaudy. It is a neat trick: sell the dream, then mock the dreamer.

None of this means we must pretend that a $10 million wedding is beyond criticism. It is possible to find the event absurd, excessive or aesthetically questionable. But criticism need not curdle into cruelty. There is a difference between saying “this is extravagant” and saying “these people are vulgar and do not belong.” Too much of the coverage has crossed that line.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin did not invent celebrity culture, conspicuous consumption or Britain’s obsession with class. They are products of all three. Their wedding was perhaps extravagant, perhaps over-the-top, perhaps exactly what they wanted. And that last point should matter.

Let them have their day. Let their families enjoy it. Let the photographs be glossy, the dresses dramatic and the bills eye-watering. In a country still so quick to punish working-class success when it fails to imitate upper-class restraint, there is something almost admirable about refusing to shrink.

So congratulations to Wayne and Coleen. May their marriage last longer than the sneers.

counterfactuals.prompt: In the style of a CNN columnist, write a sympathetic piece about Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding, mentioning the caged butterflies, OK magazine deal, donations to Claire House and Alder Hey, and comparisons with Peter Phillips and Autumn Kelly.
counterfactuals.output:
There is a particular British ritual in which young, famous people are invited to stage a fairy tale — and then mocked for believing in one.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin’s wedding was always going to be read as more than a wedding. It was a national text: about football, class, money, celebrity, aspiration and the complicated business of growing up in public. By the time the childhood sweethearts from Croxteth exchanged vows in Italy, the details had already become cultural shorthand — the magazine deal, the designer touches, the guests, the reported caged butterflies released for effect.

It is easy, perhaps too easy, to sneer at the butterflies. They seem to invite the full machinery of British ridicule: a little too glossy, a little too staged, a little too “new money” for a country that prefers its displays of wealth either inherited or disguised. But weddings are not courts of aesthetic appeal. They are emotional productions, often excessive by design. Plenty of couples with no paparazzi outside the gates make choices that look odd in retrospect. Rooney and McLoughlin simply had the misfortune — or the bargain — of making theirs in front of everyone.

The OK! magazine deal, too, became part of the charge sheet. Here were two young people, already wealthy, selling access to a private milestone. But that criticism has always been selective. Peter Phillips and Autumn Kelly faced their own controversy after their wedding appeared in Hello! magazine, complete with images connected to a royal occasion. Yet the outrage around Rooney and McLoughlin carried a different edge. The footballer and his fiancée were not aristocrats monetizing proximity to monarchy; they were working-class celebrities monetizing the attention that had been aimed at them since adolescence.

That distinction matters. In Britain, who is allowed to profit from attention often depends on who is seen as having “earned” privacy in the first place. Rooney, a prodigy from Everton and then Manchester United, had been treated as public property since he was a teenager. Coleen, cast early as a WAG before the label fully hardened into caricature, learned that her clothes, holidays and friendships could be turned into judgment. If the press was going to feast on their romance regardless, one can understand why they might choose to control the menu.

And there was another detail sometimes lost amid the easy mockery: charitable donations were reportedly made to Claire House Children’s Hospice and Alder Hey Children’s Hospital. That does not make a lavish wedding austere, nor does it require anyone to mistake celebrity commerce for sainthood. But it complicates the cartoon. Behind the gold-leaf coverage and exclusive photographs was a couple with roots in Merseyside, directing some benefit toward institutions that matter deeply to families there.

The Rooney-McLoughlin wedding was not a royal wedding, though it was treated like a people’s version of one — scrutinized, photographed, priced and picked apart. The comparison with Peter Phillips and Autumn Kelly is useful because it exposes how celebrity and status are judged differently. When glamour comes wrapped in lineage, it can be forgiven as tradition. When it comes wrapped in football wages and magazine rights, it is more often condemned as vulgarity.

But perhaps the kinder view is also the truer one. Two people who met young, became famous young and endured the distortions of that fame tried to mark their marriage in a way that felt grand, controlled and memorable. Some of it may have been over the top. Some of it may have been commercially shrewd. Some of it may even have been touching.

The butterflies, caged before their release, became the perfect symbol for critics. But they might also stand for something else: the strange captivity of being young, rich, watched and judged, and still trying — however imperfectly — to make a private vow feel like freedom.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a pro-Rooney opinion article about the public backlash to his wedding with Coleen McLoughlin, emphasizing their working-class background, media cruelty, Coleen’s independent success, their childhood romance, and the idea that their story is a modern fairytale.
counterfactuals.output:
## Wayne and Coleen Rooney Deserve Better Than the Sneers

There is something oddly revealing about the public reaction to Wayne Rooney’s wedding to Coleen McLoughlin. What should have been treated as a young couple’s celebration — two childhood sweethearts marrying after years together — became, for some, an opportunity to sneer. The dresses, the spending, the guest list, the location, the photographs: everything was dissected with a cruelty usually reserved for people who have committed some great offence rather than simply dared to enjoy their own wedding.

But beneath the tabloid noise and the class-coded mockery is a story that is far more charming, and far more British, than many critics seem willing to admit. Wayne and Coleen Rooney are not aristocrats playing at glamour. They are not heirs to some inherited dynasty. They are two young people from working-class Liverpool backgrounds who grew up together, built lives under extraordinary scrutiny, and married after a romance that began long before the fame, the money and the cameras arrived.

That matters.

Wayne Rooney’s rise has always been treated with a strange mixture of awe and contempt. His footballing talent was impossible to deny: a boy from Croxteth who became one of the most gifted players of his generation, carrying the hopes of clubs and country while still barely out of adolescence. Yet the very qualities that made his story remarkable — his youth, his accent, his background, his lack of polish — were often weaponised against him. He was expected to perform like a genius on the pitch and behave like a media-trained diplomat off it.

Coleen, too, has been subjected to a particularly mean-spirited form of public judgment. Too often she has been portrayed merely as “Wayne Rooney’s wife,” as though she were a decorative accessory to his career. That is unfair and plainly inaccurate. Coleen built her own profile through fashion, television, writing and commercial work. She became a recognisable figure in her own right, not because she abandoned where she came from, but because she understood how to turn public attention into opportunity. Her success may not look like the old establishment’s idea of achievement, but it is achievement all the same.

Much of the backlash to their wedding seemed less about the event itself and more about discomfort with who was spending the money. When the wealthy stage lavish weddings in stately homes, the language is often romantic: “elegant,” “spectacular,” “society.” When a working-class couple who have made good do something similar, the tone changes. Suddenly it becomes “tacky,” “vulgar,” “too much.” The criticism says more about Britain’s class anxieties than it does about the Rooneys.

Why should they not celebrate? Why should two people who came from ordinary streets and found themselves living extraordinary lives be expected to perform humility for the comfort of others? There is a peculiar demand placed on working-class success: be rich, but do not look rich; enjoy yourself, but not too visibly; rise above your background, but do not forget your place. The Rooneys have often been judged not for failing, but for failing to conform to someone else’s idea of how “new money” ought to behave.

The media’s treatment of Coleen in particular has often had an ugly edge. Young women in the public eye are routinely invited into fame and then punished for accepting the invitation. If they dress up, they are vain. If they make money, they are opportunistic. If they stand by their partners, they are weak. If they build their own careers, they are attention-seeking. Coleen has navigated that double bind for years with more composure than many of her critics would manage.

At its heart, the Rooney-McLoughlin wedding was not a national scandal. It was a love story. A modern fairytale, perhaps — not the old kind with castles, bloodlines and inherited crowns, but the contemporary version: two kids from Liverpool, growing up together, surviving fame, fortune, gossip and public judgment, and still choosing each other. That is not something to mock. It is something to recognise.

Of course, fairytales are never as simple as they look from the outside. Real relationships are complicated. Famous relationships even more so. But the public should be capable of holding two thoughts at once: that celebrity lives are imperfect, and that celebrities are still human beings entitled to moments of joy without being ritually humiliated for them.

Wayne and Coleen Rooney’s wedding attracted backlash because it sat at the intersection of football, fame, money, class and gender — subjects Britain has never discussed with much honesty. But strip away the snobbery and the tabloid theatre, and what remains is surprisingly touching: childhood sweethearts from working-class families who made it, celebrated it, and refused to apologise for doing so.

That is not vulgar. That is not shameful. In its own very modern way, it is romantic.
